title: Word families
statement:
A word game groups tiles into families: two words belong to the same family if one can be made by rearranging all the letters of the other.

Given a list of lowercase `words`, return the families as a list of lists. The families can be in any order, and the words inside a family can be in any order. Every word belongs to exactly one family, and repeated words stay in the same family.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are words only lowercase letters?
clarifyingQuestions.why: A fixed 26-letter alphabet allows a letter-count key instead of sorting.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the list or a word be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The list can be empty, which returns an empty list. An empty string is a valid word and forms its own family with other empty strings.
clarifyingQuestions.why: Base cases that break code assuming at least one letter.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do repeated words stay together?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, duplicates go in the same family and are both kept.
clarifyingQuestions.why: Rules out deduplicating with a set.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the order of families or words matter?
clarifyingQuestions.why: Frees you from sorting the output.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many words, and how long?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 10,000 words, each up to 100 letters.
clarifyingQuestions.why: Sets the cost of building a key per word.

hiddenConstraints: Up to 10,000 words of up to 100 lowercase letters.

edgeCases.why: Same letters, different counts: not a family.
Duplicates stay in one family, both kept.

approaches.name: Compare every pair
approaches.idea: For each word, compare it with every existing family by checking whether they are rearrangements.
approaches.tradeoffs: Simple but quadratic in the number of words.

approaches.name: Hash by sorted letters
approaches.idea: Two words are rearrangements exactly when their sorted letters are equal. Use the sorted word as a key in a hash map of lists.
approaches.tradeoffs: Linear in the number of words; sorting each word costs k log k.

approaches.name: Hash by letter counts
approaches.idea: Use a tuple of 26 letter counts as the key.
approaches.tradeoffs: Removes the log factor; the 26-length key is a constant cost. Worth it only for long words.

optimal.name: Hash map keyed by a canonical form
optimal.explanation: Pick a canonical form that is identical for rearrangements: the sorted letters, or the 26 letter counts. Map each canonical form to the list of words that share it, then return the lists.
optimal.time: O(n * k log k) with sorting, O(n * k) with counts

hintLadder: What do two rearranged words have in common, no matter the order of their letters?
Could you turn each word into something that is identical for every member of its family?
Once every word has that form, how could you collect words that share it?
Sort each word’s letters and use the result as a hash map key whose value is the list of words.

expectedMentions.what: Asks about the character set or case
Explains that rearrangements share a canonical form such as sorted letters
States the complexity in terms of the number of words and word length
Compares sorting each word with counting letters
Traces an example, including a near-miss like "ab" and "aab"

followUps: Words can contain any Unicode characters. Which key still works?
Return only families with at least two words, largest first.
vocabulary: O of n k log k

walkthrough.say: Are the words all lowercase letters? Can there be empty strings, and what about duplicates, do I keep both copies?
And the order of the families in the output doesn’t matter, right?

Comparing every word with every family would be quadratic in the number of words. Instead, I want a key that’s the same for any rearrangement. If I sort the letters of stop, pots and tops, they all become o, p, s, t.
So I’ll use a hash map from sorted letters to a list of words. With n words of length up to k, sorting each word is k log k, so overall n times k log k time and n times k space to hold the output.
The map’s values are the families. setdefault creates the list the first time a key appears.
Tracing stop, pots, tops, cat, act, dog: the first three get key opst, cat and act get act, dog gets dgo. Three families, which matches.
A near miss: ab and aab sort to ab and aab, which differ, so they stay apart. Good. And an empty string sorts to an empty key, so two empty strings share a family.
If words were very long, I could key by a tuple of 26 letter counts to avoid sorting, which makes it n times k. For short words, sorting is simpler.
